title: AgentTwin Guide: Testing Duplicate Writes and Forbidden Side Effects
content:
A retry can create a duplicate even when every response looks successful. Two workers can also deliver the same operation at once. A single-failure test catches one version of that bug; it does not prove the workflow is safe when requests overlap.

This guide shows how to test that distinction with **AgentTwin**, a developer tool for prepared Node.js application and AI-agent workflows. The test needs an explicit starting state, a supported failure and final-state assertions.

## Why one successful call is not enough

Suppose a workflow creates a customer notification after recording a payment. The first run reaches the notification endpoint once, returns 200 and leaves the expected record. That run is evidence for one execution. It does not establish that a duplicate delivery is harmless, or that a retry after a lost response cannot create a second record.

AgentTwin's [fault documentation](https://agenttwin.si/docs/wedge/) separates four supported behaviors: timeout-after-write, blackhole, server-error and duplicate-write. The first three are not interchangeable with duplicate delivery. A test should name the condition it is exercising.

## Declare the state and the damage

A useful duplicate-write test declares more than a successful response. It needs:

- a synthetic starting state with the records the workflow will use;
- the exact operation that must happen once;
- a supported fault that exposes duplicate delivery;
- required final-state assertions;
- forbidden effects and preserved records that must remain unchanged.

The [evidence guide](https://agenttwin.si/docs/evidence/) distinguishes required outcomes, `forbiddenEffects` and `preservedState`. A workflow that creates the expected ticket but also changes a protected customer record fails the safety check. That is stronger evidence than a green process exit.

## Build a duplicate-write test

Start with the synthetic example from the [AgentTwin quickstart](https://agenttwin.si/docs/quickstart/). Read the generated files before execution. The clean run expects one ticket and one notification. The faulted run exposes a duplicate ticket when the workflow retries after a lost response.

For a duplicate-delivery test, keep the same declared checks and choose the supported duplicate-write behavior only when the prepared workflow and operation contracts cover it. Do not relabel a timeout as a duplicate-write test. An untriggered requested fault means the intended condition was not tested.

Record the starting records, observed operations, final state and assertion results. Then reset the test world and rerun the same world. A reset clears mutable state, idempotency keys, events and fault activation, so the second run starts from a comparable baseline.

## Assertions that catch unwanted damage

A practical check set might require exactly one notification and one payment update. Add a forbidden effect for a second notification write, and preserve the customer record that the workflow must not modify. The exact service names and paths must match the prepared operation contracts.

[AgentTwin](https://agenttwin.si/what-is-agenttwin/) records state changes and assertion results so a developer can inspect what happened. It does not copy every production condition or provide a universal provider clone. Local runs also have host filesystem and network access; review application files and credentials before running them.

## Repair the source, keep the checks

When the duplicate appears, inspect the first failing assertion and the operation timeline. Fix the application's idempotency or delivery handling in its original repository. Keep the scenario, fault and checks unchanged, then run the same world again and compare receipts.

A source digest should change; the specification and scenario digests should remain fixed. A passing rerun is evidence that this prepared workflow avoids the declared duplicate in this test world. It is not proof of production equivalence or every provider's behavior.

Use the [workflow guides](https://agenttwin.si/guides/) for more examples and the [provider operation contracts](https://agenttwin.si/docs/provider-operations/) to check what the current test world actually models.
excerpt: A duplicate write can survive a successful response. Test concurrent delivery with synthetic state, final-state assertions and forbidden effects.

title: When 200 OK Is Not Success: Testing Retry Safety with Final-State Checks
content:
A payment API can return **200 OK** and still leave a workflow in the wrong state. A customer is charged twice after a timeout. A webhook arrives twice after a network retry. The response looks successful, but the final records tell a different story.

That is why an HTTP mock on its own is often not enough. You need to control the response timing and inspect the state left behind by the workflow.

## A concrete retry-safety test

Start with one payment intent. Run the workflow once and assert one charge and one receipt. Then introduce a timeout after the write commits. The write happened, but the caller did not receive a response. If the application retries without an idempotency key, a second charge can appear.

In [AgentTwin's synthetic ticket example](https://agenttwin.si/docs/quickstart/), the clean run expects one ticket and one notification. The faulted run uses `timeout-after-write`, and the duplicate ticket is the failure. The goal is not to make every provider behave like production; it is to make one supported failure reproducible and visible.

## Check the state, not only the exit code

A test passes only when its declared outcomes and forbidden effects are true. Record the initial state, the operations observed, the final records and the assertion results. A successful process exit does not prove that the workflow avoided a duplicate side effect.

For the retry scenario, check both sides of the contract:

- the required customer charge exists exactly once;
- no extra refund, notification or ledger entry was created;
- replaying the same seed and fault reproduces the failure;
- changing the application logic while keeping the checks unchanged makes the failure disappear.

## Where the tool fits

[AgentTwin](https://agenttwin.si/what-is-agenttwin/) is for testing prepared Node.js application and AI-agent workflows against synthetic service data and supported failures. It runs the workflow locally by default and records the observed state. It is not a full network-isolation sandbox, a universal provider clone or a production-equivalence guarantee.

That limited scope is useful. You can start with one known workflow, one declared failure and one final-state check. Later, add a second service, a reset, a replay or a regression. The test world grows with the evidence you actually have.

## Practical checklist

1. Choose a write that should happen once even when its response is lost.
2. Declare the starting records and the exact final state you expect.
3. Add a check for unwanted side effects, not only the happy-path result.
4. Introduce the supported failure and keep the assertions unchanged.
5. Save the failing run, repair the application and replay against the same checks.
6. State what the test covers and what remains unverified.

The useful output is a receipt you can inspect, not a green label that hides the state. Read the [workflow testing guides](https://agenttwin.si/guides/) for reset and duplicate-event examples.
excerpt: A successful HTTP response can hide a duplicate write. Test lost responses with a declared starting state, fault injection and final-state assertions instead.

title: Venture Capital Trends Shift Towards Sustainability and Technology
content:
Recent trends in venture capital investments are highlighting a clear shift towards technology and sustainability-focused startups. The data from the first quarter of 2021 shows a significant increase in funding for companies in these sectors, signaling a potential change in investor preferences and strategies.

The first quarter of 2021 witnessed a record-breaking $125 billion of venture capital investments worldwide. This represents a 94% increase compared to the same period last year. A significant portion of this funding was directed towards technology and sustainability-focused startups, which have been gaining increasing attention from investors.

The technology sector, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and FinTech, has seen a considerable surge in funding. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the digital transformation in many industries, leading to increased demand for innovative tech solutions. As a result, venture capitalists are investing more heavily in tech startups, viewing them as key players in the post-pandemic world.

Similarly, sustainability-focused startups, particularly in the renewable energy, food technology, and electric vehicle sectors, have also received substantial funding. This trend is driven by a growing global awareness of climate change and the urgent need for sustainable solutions. Venture capitalists are recognizing the potential profitability of these sectors, as well as their importance for the future of the planet.

This shift in venture capital trends is expected to have significant implications for startups and investors alike. For startups, it signals a need to align their business models with investor preferences for technology and sustainability. For investors, it suggests a need to stay informed about developments in these sectors to make strategic investment decisions.

Looking ahead, these trends are expected to continue, as technology and sustainability become increasingly important in a post-pandemic world. The venture capital landscape is likely to evolve further, with new investment strategies and opportunities emerging in response to global challenges and market needs.
excerpt: Venture capital trends are increasingly leaning towards technology and sustainability-focused startups. The first quarter of 2021 saw record-breaking investments in these sectors, indicating a significant shift in investor strategies and preferences.
